title: Behind Project Suncatcher, our moonshot to put AI in space
gist: Google's Project Suncatcher is launching its first prototype satellite (on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare, built with Planet) to test whether Trillium TPUs can survive launch, radiation and vacuum cooling, as a first step toward orbital AI compute powered by near-constant sunlight. Ground tests show TPUs survived launch-level vibration and radiation doses beyond a five-year mission; the next milestone is a two-satellite laser-interconnect test in 2027.

insights.claim: Google is pursuing space-based AI compute because satellites in low Earth orbit get near-constant sunlight and can generate up to eight times more solar power than panels on Earth.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Signals hyperscalers view terrestrial power as a binding constraint on AI scaling; watch space-solar and orbital data-center supply chains as a long-dated optionality theme.
insights.quote: In low Earth orbit, satellites can access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth.
insights.locator: After years of research, Project Suncatcher

insights.claim: Google frames Project Suncatcher as a long-term research moonshot comparable to its early autonomous driving and quantum computing efforts, implying years of experimentation before any practical orbital AI system.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Treat orbital AI compute as a multi-year R&D bet with no near-term revenue impact on Alphabet; it is optionality, not capacity.
insights.quote: Just as early research into autonomous driving and quantum computing required years of experimentation before we got to practical systems, exploring compute in space begins with measured, deliberate steps.
insights.locator: Big breakthroughs happen when you work backwards

insights.claim: Google's long-run vision for Project Suncatcher is to link multiple constellations of TPU-carrying satellites so they can jointly run larger AI workloads in orbit.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: If realized, orbital clusters would require large satellite volumes and launch cadence, a potential demand driver for launch providers and satellite builders.
insights.locator: After years of research, Project Suncatcher

insights.claim: Project Suncatcher's first prototype satellite, developed in partnership with Planet, flies on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission to gather in-orbit data on how Google TPUs handle spaceflight stress, radiation and thermal extremes.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Planet gains a marquee hyperscaler partnership for hosted compute payloads; SpaceX rideshare remains the default access path for experimental orbital hardware.
insights.locator: Turning that idea into reality starts with a basic question

insights.claim: Google's first Suncatcher TPUs were slated to reach orbit the week after the September 24, 2026 announcement, with the next milestone targeted for 2027.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Near-term catalyst: in-orbit results from the prototype could move sentiment on space-compute names (Planet, launch providers) over the following months.
insights.quote: Putting our first TPUs in orbit next week will help us get data and learnings to inform future launches.
insights.locator: But some things can only be tested in space

insights.claim: The first Suncatcher launch is explicitly a learning mission meant to identify points of failure before scaling, not a production deployment of orbital compute.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Temper expectations: failures in this test would be consistent with plan and not necessarily kill the program.
insights.quote: This first launch is about seeing what works, identifying points of failure, and applying those findings to future missions.

insights.claim: A rocket trip to low Earth orbit lasts about 10 minutes with sustained acceleration up to 10 g, while individual components such as TPU chips can experience 50 to 100 g.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Quantifies the ruggedization bar commercial AI accelerators must clear to be space-deployable.

insights.claim: Google's Suncatcher satellite survived three-axis vibration testing mimicking rocket-launch frequencies, a result the team described as a pleasant surprise.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Suggests commodity-derived datacenter accelerators may need less custom hardening than assumed, lowering cost of orbital compute.
insights.quote: Tests like this rarely go as planned, so we were pleasantly surprised that the hardware held up to the force.

insights.claim: In proton-beam testing at UC Davis's Crocker Nuclear Laboratory while running AI workloads, Google's Trillium TPUs survived a total ionizing radiation dose greater than they would receive over a five-year space mission.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: A five-year radiation tolerance for off-the-shelf datacenter TPUs supports a plausible multi-year depreciation life for orbital compute assets, key to the economics.
insights.quote: Initial results have shown that our Trillium TPUs hold up remarkably well, and can survive a radiation total ionizing dose greater than what they would receive during a five-year space mission.
insights.locator: Once the TPU chips make it to space

insights.claim: Beyond total dose, Google is monitoring how radiation-induced errors such as bitflips from solar events and cosmic rays affect AI workloads running on TPUs.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Soft-error tolerance of ML workloads, not just chip survival, will determine whether orbital compute is usable; watch for results on error rates.
insights.locator: Once the TPU chips make it to space

insights.claim: Cooling is a central unsolved problem for orbital data centers because with no airflow in a vacuum, heat from densely packed TPUs can only be shed via radiators.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Thermal management (radiator mass and area) is likely the key cost and scale limiter for space compute; a niche for thermal-hardware suppliers.
insights.quote: In a vacuum, you can only diffuse heat via radiators, which requires a totally different approach to cooling electronics.

insights.claim: Google is testing a TPU cooling system combining heat pipes and radiators, validated so far only in a thermal vacuum chamber, with in-orbit performance still unknown.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: The prototype's thermal data is the key readout to watch for whether orbital compute density is viable.
insights.locator: We're working on a number of different approaches

insights.claim: Future Suncatcher satellites are planned to each carry dozens of TPU chips and orbit in clusters linked by lasers, requiring each satellite to know its position relative to its neighbors.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Implies demand for precise formation-flying and optical inter-satellite link technology.

insights.claim: Existing space laser links are optimized for low bandwidth over long distances, whereas orbital AI clusters need very high bandwidth over extremely short distances, a gap Google must engineer across.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: Current optical-terminal vendors' products do not directly fit the orbital-AI use case; a new product category may emerge.
insights.quote: most state-of-the-art systems are optimized for low bandwidth across large distances, whereas our lasers need to operate at very high bandwidth over extremely short distances

insights.claim: Google plans to test high-bandwidth short-range laser links between satellites in 2027 by putting two satellites in orbit.
insights.speaker: Travis Beals
insights.so_what: 2027 two-satellite test is the next dated catalyst for evaluating orbital AI cluster feasibility.
insights.quote: We'll test our work on this in 2027 when we put two satellites in orbit.
